The **Iași National Theatre** (or **Vasile Alecsandri National Theater**; in [Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"): Teatrul Național Vasile Alecsandri) in [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași"), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania"), is the oldest national theatre and one of the most prestigious theatrical institutions in Romania. In 1956, it was given the name of the renowned Romanian playwright and poet [Vasile Alecsandri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Alecsandri "Vasile Alecsandri"). The building also hosts the [Iași Romanian National Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_Romanian_National_Opera "Iași Romanian National Opera").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/TNI_1846.jpg/250px-TNI_1846.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TNI_1846.jpg)

The old building of the National Theatre, 1846

The first dramatic play presented in the Romanian language (and one of the first theatrical performance in Romanian[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-3)) was _Mirtil and Hloe_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-Gessner1850-4) adapted and staged by [Gheorghe Asachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gheorghe_Asachi "Gheorghe Asachi"), and held in the capital (Jassy/Iași) of [Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia "Moldavia"), on 27 December 1816.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-5) In 1834, a Romanian production took place in Iași on the stage of the [Théâtre de varieté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_des_Vari%C3%A9t%C3%A9s_(Ia%C8%99i) "Théâtre des Variétés (Iași)"), built in 1832 for the French Fouraux troupe.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The National Theatre was founded on 15 May 1840, as the _Great Theatre of Moldavia_, when the Romanian language troupe, led by [Costache Caragiali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costache_Caragiale "Costache Caragiale"), was united with the French troupe, under a single direction of [Vasile Alecsandri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Alecsandri "Vasile Alecsandri") and the management of Costache Caragiali.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-6) On 22 December 1846, a new audience hall was inaugurated in the former mansion of [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Moldavia "List of rulers of Moldavia")[Mihail Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Sturdza "Mihail Sturdza"), on the [Hill of Copou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_hills_of_Ia%C8%99i "Seven hills of Iași").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-7)

## Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Building")]

On the night of 17/18 February 1888, the theatre building was destroyed by the fire. Efforts to build the new theatre edifice culminated in 1894 when a contract was signed with the Viennese architects [Ferdinand Fellner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Fellner "Ferdinand Fellner") and [Hermann Helmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Helmer "Hermann Helmer"), who designed several theatres and palaces across Europe, including the theatres in [Cluj-Napoca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cluj-Napoca_National_Theatre "Cluj-Napoca National Theatre"), [Oradea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oradea "Oradea"), [Timișoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timi%C8%99oara "Timișoara") and [Chernivtsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernivtsi "Chernivtsi") (Romanian: Cernăuți).

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Teatrul_Na%C5%A3ional_Interior.jpg/250px-Teatrul_Na%C5%A3ional_Interior.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Teatrul_Na%C5%A3ional_Interior.jpg)

The main auditorium

For the building work, a contract was signed with a Bucharest company, and the power station was built by a company from Berlin. The Theatre’s power station also supplied with electricity the 12 electric-arc lamps lighting the Theatre Square, marking the beginning of electrification in the city of Iași. The works to building took two years, and on 1 and 2 December 1896, the inauguration festivities took place with [Flechtenmacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Flechtenmacher?action=edit&redlink=1 "Alexander Flechtenmacher (page does not exist)")'s _National Overture_, the vaudevilles _Muza de la Burdujeni_ (_The Muse from Burdujeni_) by [Costache Negruzzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costache_Negruzzi "Costache Negruzzi") and _Cinel-cinel_ (_The Riddle_) by Vasile Alecsandri, as well as the verse comedy _Poetul romantic_ (_The Romantic Poet_) by [Matei Millo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matei_Millo "Matei Millo").

The Iași National Theatre building is listed in the [National Register of Historic Monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Monuments_in_Romania "National Register of Historic Monuments in Romania").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-8)

### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architecture")]

With a [Neoclassic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassic_style "Neoclassic style") exterior and a richly decorated interior in [Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo "Rococo") and [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") styles, the building is considered one of the most elegant in Romania.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-9)

The main auditorium is organised in stalls, boxes and a balcony. The curtain painted by the Viennese M. Lenz, presents in the middle, an allegory of life with its three stages and, to the right side, the allegory of [Romanian Unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Romania "Greater Romania"). The left-hand side, painted by Lenz’s apprentice, differs from the rest of the curtain in style and colouring.

The ceiling and the iron curtain were painted by Alexander Goltz. The iron curtain, which completely separates the scene from the hall, shows ornaments placed symmetrically, while the ceiling has as a narrative basis the Archetypal Story, shown in paradisiacal allegories, with nymphs and cupids framed in rococo stucco.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-10)

The 1,418 electric lights and the chandelier with 109 Venetian crystal lamps light up the playhouse.

It gets in touch with an agency that has a network of clients with high income customers (such as high-end supermarkets) and asks the agency to create profiles of young parents or couples who can be assumed to be wealthy and to have a new child, so that these can later be used to present advertising within partner apps based on those profiles.

Who Comédie Française

When 1680 

 Founded in 1680 by Louis XIV, the Comédie Française is the oldest National Theatre in the world. During the Revolution (1789) the company split: the conservatives went to the Théâtre de la Nation, the more revolutionary actors became the Théâtre de la République at the Palais Royal. In 1803 the Comédie Française was reformed and has remained in being ever since.

The foyer of Dublin's historic Abbey Theatre is full of middle-aged Goths. Nick Cave is playing an intimate show tonight on a set designed for _Ulysses_ – so these fans hope to sit on stage, close to their idol, at the theatrical cabaret tables gathered around what is usually a pretend Dublin pub.

James Joyce's famously difficult-to-finish 1000-page novel about 24 hours in the life of Dublin has been comically abridged for stage by Dermot Bolger – and features lots of puppets.

Puppets? Nick Cave? Comedy?

Actually, James Hickson points out (ironically since we're in the Irish capital), the Abbey is "the oldest national theatre in the English-speaking world".

Two years after the Irish Free State was formed in 1922 (before becoming the Republic of Ireland in 1937), the newly-formed government began subsidising the Abbey as a crucible of Irish culture.

And yet the Abbey was already promoting Irish culture, long before the Easter Rising of 1916 or the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921.

"In fact, this was our national theatre before Ireland became an independent nation," says Hickson.

Hickson – a lecturer at Trinity College's Samuel Beckett Centre as well as the Abbey's chief theatre guide – is explaining the rich heritage of the Abbey in its WB Yeats Lounge, named after the great poet and one of the Abbey's key creators.

Other portraits line the lounge (which serves as the main interval bar). Though some are actors or directors, most are playwrights whose work has been performed here.

There's John Millington Synge (_Playboy of the Western World_), Lady Augusta Gregory (_Spreading the News_), Sean O'Casey (_Juno and the Paycock, The Plough and the Stars_), Brendan Behan (_The Quare Fellow_).

Two of those plays caused riots, Hickson explains.

The theatre was also part of a rebellion/liberation campaign, had its ornate exterior destroyed by a diverted bus driver, and was almost burnt to a crisp in the 1950s. But perhaps we should let Hickson go back to the beginning …

The theatre (Amharclann na Mainistreach in Irish) opened in December 1904 in the former Mechanics Hall in Lower Abbey Street, as a venue for Irish theatre. The first night consisted of three one-act plays: _On Baile's Strand_ by Yeats, _Spreading the News_ by Lady Gregory, and _Kathleen ni Houlihan_, co-written by Yeats and Gregory.

By then, Oscar Wilde was dead and George Bernard Shaw was based in the English home counties.

But Yeats, Lady Gregory, Synge and playwright Edward Martyn (the first president of Sinn Fein) were determined to inspire an Irish literary revival.

Another crucial character in the theatre's history was an Englishwoman, Annie Horniman (whose portrait also resides in the WB Yeats Lounge).

"She was the financier," Hickson says. Born in Manchester, Horniman had theatrical experience (she'd been involved in Shaw's _Arms_ _and the Man_) and had arrived in Dublin as Yeats' unpaid assistant).

Scandal struck the Abbey in January 1907 when it became the scene of "the Playboy Riots".

"A guy walks into a bar," Hickson begins, explaining why the first night of _Playboy of the Western World_ proved so important to world theatre.

"I'm paraphrasing, but he says, 'I've had an argument with my father and I've killed him'. The assumption of the audience is that this is a law-abiding, god-fearing rural community in western Ireland and they'll hand him into the authorities…

"Lady Gregory sent Yeats a telegram in the interval: 'Play great success'."

However, the telegram proved premature. There's a line in the play about "a drift of females standing in their shifts".

"A shift, in Irish, meant female nightwear," Hickson explains. In retrospect, the riot was clearly premeditated, organised by Irish nationalists who felt the play was not sufficiently political and a slur on the fidelity of Irish women.

"People went crazy," Hickson says. "Irishwomen were supposed to be so virtuous they would never be seen in their nightwear.

"No matter that there was a young doctor who said he'd had to stop himself from standing up and pointing to all the men and women in the audience he was treating for sexually transmitted diseases."

Two decades went by before the next riot.

"O'Casey's _The Plough and the Stars_ was written ten years after the Easter Rising, but it's about the Easter Rising," Hickson continues. "The question it poses is: was it worth it? That was controversial. People died."

Members of the Abbey Theatre – actors, writers, stage crew – also took part in the Easter Rising. There's a plaque commemorating them in the foyer.

One was the poet Peadar Kearney, who wrote the lyrics to _The Soldier's Song_ (now the Irish national anthem) in 1907. A stage assistant and occasional actor, Kearney quit an Abbey theatre tour of England to take part in the Rising, fighting at the Jacob's biscuit factory. He was later interned by the British during the War of Independence.

There were no more riots at the Abbey – only a devastating fire in 1951. For 15 years, the theatre company operated (again ironically) out of the city's now demolished Queen's Theatre (named after Victoria).

During that time, the artistic director would check the derelict building regularly.

"Once he heard a suspicious noise, tap-tap-tap," Hickson says. "He went along the corridor to investigate and opened the door …

"There was Brendan Behan, using it as an unpaid office because he'd got spare keys."

The national theatre returned to Lower Abbey Street in 1966.

Since then, a new breed of Irish playwrights have had their work pioneered at the Abbey.

Brian Friel (_Dancing at Lughnasa_), Tom Murphy (_The Gigli Concert_), Hugh Leonard (_Da_) and Marina Carr (_Bog of Cats_) have all seen their work expand to Broadway and London's West End.

More are to come, Hickson says. The Abbey is just as alive and relevant now as it was more than a century ago.

## FIVE OTHER HISTORIC THEATRES YOU SHOULD SEE

### TEATRO AMAZONAS, MANAUS, BRAZIL

In the middle of Brazil's Amazon rainforest is one of the most beautiful 19th century Belle Epoque follies ever built. Paid for by "rubber barons" and designed by the exquisitely named Italian architect Celestial Sacardim, the most remote opera house in the world took 15 years to build. Best to book ahead, [visitbrasil.com/en/destinos/manaus](http://visitbrasil.com/en/destinos/manaus)

### SHAKESPEARE'S GLOBE, LONDON, UK

Sure, this isn't exactly historic since it was only opened in 1997, a labour of love (and money) by the late American actor and director, Sam Wanamaker. But it is a near-as-damn-it replica of the open air Globe where the first performances of _Hamlet_, _Othello_ and _Romeo and Juliet_ were seen. Fortunately, the toilets and bars are more Elizabeth II-era. See [shakespearesglobe.com](http://shakespearesglobe.com/)

### BOLSHOI THEATRE, MOSCOW, RUSSIA

Even of you know nothing about ballet, you'll have heard of the Bolshoi. Its ballet company is the biggest in the world, with more than 200 dancers – and has outlasted Czars, Bolshevik revolutions and Soviet dictators. Re-opened in 2011 after a six year renovation, it remains one of the greatest places to watch ballet – or opera! See [bolshoi.ru/en](http://bolshoi.ru/en)

### NATIONAL NOH THEATRE, TOKYO, JAPAN

Don't judge the theatre from its horrible exterior, or its youth (it was opened in 1983). This is the place to be introduced to the traditional Japanese form of song-and-dance drama which dates back to the 14th century. If you're bored, revel in the high-tech seats (with English translations) and admire the 400-year old cypress trees which make up the elaborate stage. See [ntj.jac.go.jp](http://ntj.jac.go.jp/)

### FORD'S THEATRE, WASHINGTON DC, US

Nobody would remember _Our American Cousin_, a three-act farce written by English playwright Tom Taylor, except for one thing. It was the play US President Abraham Lincoln was watching when he was assassinated by actor, Confederate zealot and white supremacist John Wilkes Booth on April 14, 1865. The theatre is still open for tours and shows. See [fords.org](http://fords.org/)

The foyer of Dublin's historic Abbey Theatre is full of middle-aged Goths. Nick Cave is playing an intimate show tonight on a set designed for _Ulysses_ – so these fans hope to sit on stage, close to their idol, at the theatrical cabaret tables gathered around what is usually a pretend Dublin pub.

James Joyce's famously difficult-to-finish 1000-page novel about 24 hours in the life of Dublin has been comically abridged for stage by Dermot Bolger – and features lots of puppets.

Puppets? Nick Cave? Comedy?

![Image 3: Dublin's historic Abbey Theatre.](link_63)

Dublin's historic Abbey Theatre.Ros Kavanagh

Clearly the Abbey isn't a typical national theatre.

Actually, James Hickson points out (ironically since we're in the Irish capital), the Abbey is "the oldest national theatre in the English-speaking world".

Two years after the Irish Free State was formed in 1922 (before becoming the Republic of Ireland in 1937), the newly-formed government began subsidising the Abbey as a crucible of Irish culture.

And yet the Abbey was already promoting Irish culture, long before the Easter Rising of 1916 or the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921.

"In fact, this was our national theatre before Ireland became an independent nation," says Hickson.

Advertisement

Hickson – a lecturer at Trinity College's Samuel Beckett Centre as well as the Abbey's chief theatre guide – is explaining the rich heritage of the Abbey in its WB Yeats Lounge, named after the great poet and one of the Abbey's key creators.

Other portraits line the lounge (which serves as the main interval bar). Though some are actors or directors, most are playwrights whose work has been performed here.

There's John Millington Synge (_Playboy of the Western World_), Lady Augusta Gregory (_Spreading the News_), Sean O'Casey (_Juno and the Paycock, The Plough and the Stars_), Brendan Behan (_The Quare Fellow_).

Two of those plays caused riots, Hickson explains.

The theatre was also part of a rebellion/liberation campaign, had its ornate exterior destroyed by a diverted bus driver, and was almost burnt to a crisp in the 1950s. But perhaps we should let Hickson go back to the beginning …

The theatre (Amharclann na Mainistreach in Irish) opened in December 1904 in the former Mechanics Hall in Lower Abbey Street, as a venue for Irish theatre. The first night consisted of three one-act plays: _On Baile's Strand_ by Yeats, _Spreading the News_ by Lady Gregory, and _Kathleen ni Houlihan_, co-written by Yeats and Gregory.

By then, Oscar Wilde was dead and George Bernard Shaw was based in the English home counties.

But Yeats, Lady Gregory, Synge and playwright Edward Martyn (the first president of Sinn Fein) were determined to inspire an Irish literary revival.

Another crucial character in the theatre's history was an Englishwoman, Annie Horniman (whose portrait also resides in the WB Yeats Lounge).

"She was the financier," Hickson says. Born in Manchester, Horniman had theatrical experience (she'd been involved in Shaw's _Arms_ _and the Man_) and had arrived in Dublin as Yeats' unpaid assistant).

Scandal struck the Abbey in January 1907 when it became the scene of "the Playboy Riots".

"A guy walks into a bar," Hickson begins, explaining why the first night of _Playboy of the Western World_ proved so important to world theatre.

"I'm paraphrasing, but he says, 'I've had an argument with my father and I've killed him'. The assumption of the audience is that this is a law-abiding, god-fearing rural community in western Ireland and they'll hand him into the authorities…

"Lady Gregory sent Yeats a telegram in the interval: 'Play great success'."

However, the telegram proved premature. There's a line in the play about "a drift of females standing in their shifts".

"A shift, in Irish, meant female nightwear," Hickson explains. In retrospect, the riot was clearly premeditated, organised by Irish nationalists who felt the play was not sufficiently political and a slur on the fidelity of Irish women.

"People went crazy," Hickson says. "Irishwomen were supposed to be so virtuous they would never be seen in their nightwear.

"No matter that there was a young doctor who said he'd had to stop himself from standing up and pointing to all the men and women in the audience he was treating for sexually transmitted diseases."

Two decades went by before the next riot.

"O'Casey's _The Plough and the Stars_ was written ten years after the Easter Rising, but it's about the Easter Rising," Hickson continues. "The question it poses is: was it worth it? That was controversial. People died."

Members of the Abbey Theatre – actors, writers, stage crew – also took part in the Easter Rising. There's a plaque commemorating them in the foyer.

One was the poet Peadar Kearney, who wrote the lyrics to _The Soldier's Song_ (now the Irish national anthem) in 1907. A stage assistant and occasional actor, Kearney quit an Abbey theatre tour of England to take part in the Rising, fighting at the Jacob's biscuit factory. He was later interned by the British during the War of Independence.

There were no more riots at the Abbey – only a devastating fire in 1951. For 15 years, the theatre company operated (again ironically) out of the city's now demolished Queen's Theatre (named after Victoria).

During that time, the artistic director would check the derelict building regularly.

"Once he heard a suspicious noise, tap-tap-tap," Hickson says. "He went along the corridor to investigate and opened the door …

"There was Brendan Behan, using it as an unpaid office because he'd got spare keys."

The national theatre returned to Lower Abbey Street in 1966.

Since then, a new breed of Irish playwrights have had their work pioneered at the Abbey.

Brian Friel (_Dancing at Lughnasa_), Tom Murphy (_The Gigli Concert_), Hugh Leonard (_Da_) and Marina Carr (_Bog of Cats_) have all seen their work expand to Broadway and London's West End.

More are to come, Hickson says. The Abbey is just as alive and relevant now as it was more than a century ago.

The **Iași National Theatre** (or **Vasile Alecsandri National Theater**; in [Romanian](link_12): Teatrul Național Vasile Alecsandri) in [Iași](link_0), [Romania](link_11), is the oldest national theatre and one of the most prestigious theatrical institutions in Romania. In 1956, it was given the name of the renowned Romanian playwright and poet [Vasile Alecsandri](link_13). The building also hosts the [Iași Romanian National Opera](link_14).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/TNI_1846.jpg/250px-TNI_1846.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TNI_1846.jpg)

The old building of the National Theatre, 1846

The first dramatic play presented in the Romanian language (and one of the first theatrical performance in Romanian[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-3)) was _Mirtil and Hloe_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-Gessner1850-4) adapted and staged by [Gheorghe Asachi](link_15), and held in the capital (Jassy/Iași) of [Moldavia](link_16), on 27 December 1816.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-5) In 1834, a Romanian production took place in Iași on the stage of the [Théâtre de varieté](link_17), built in 1832 for the French Fouraux troupe.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The National Theatre was founded on 15 May 1840, as the _Great Theatre of Moldavia_, when the Romanian language troupe, led by [Costache Caragiali](link_18), was united with the French troupe, under a single direction of [Vasile Alecsandri](link_13) and the management of Costache Caragiali.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-6) On 22 December 1846, a new audience hall was inaugurated in the former mansion of [Prince](link_19)[Mihail Sturdza](link_20), on the [Hill of Copou](link_21).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre#cite_note-7)

## Building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Building")]

[![Image 8: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre "Special:EditPage/Iași National Theatre") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability").

_Find sources:_["Iași National Theatre"](https://www.google.com/search?as_eq=wikipedia&q=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22)–[news](https://www.google.com/search?tbm=nws&q=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22+-wikipedia&tbs=ar:1)**·**[newspapers](https://www.google.com/search?&q=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22&tbs=bkt:s&tbm=bks)**·**[books](https://www.google.com/search?tbs=bks:1&q=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22+-wikipedia)**·**[scholar](https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22)**·**[JSTOR](https://www.jstor.org/action/doBasicSearch?Query=%22Ia%C8%99i+National+Theatre%22&acc=on&wc=on)_(October 2022)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

**Iași** ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English"): [/ˈ j æ ʃ(i)/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_YASH(-ee)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-7)[US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/ˈ j ɑː ʃ(i)/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_YAHSH(-ee)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-MW-9)Romanian:[[ˈjaʃʲ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Romanian "Help:IPA/Romanian")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/99/Iasi.ogg/Iasi.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iasi.ogg "File:Iasi.ogg"); also known by other [alternative names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#Etymology_and_names)), also sometimes referred to historically as **Jassy**[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-SaurerLanzinger2006-11) ([UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English "British English"): [/ˈ j æ s i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_YASS-ee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-12)[US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English "American English"): [/ˈ j ɑː s i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_YAH-see_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-MW-9)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-13)), is the [third most-populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_Romania "Cities in Romania") in [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania") and the seat of [Iași County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_County "Iași County"). Located in the historical region of [Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Moldavia "Western Moldavia"), it has traditionally been one of the leading centres of Romanian social, cultural, academic and artistic life. The city was the capital of the [Principality of Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Moldavia "Principality of Moldavia") from 1564 to 1859, then of the [United Principalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Principalities "United Principalities") from 1859 to 1862, and the capital of [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Romania "Kingdom of Romania") from 1916 to 1918.

Known as the Cultural Capital of Romania, Iași is a symbol of Romanian history. Historian [Nicolae Iorga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Iorga "Nicolae Iorga") stated that "there should be no Romanian who does not know of it."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-14) Still referred to as "The Moldavian Capital," Iași is the main economic and business centre of Romania's Moldavian region.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-15) In December 2018, Iași was officially declared the Historical Capital of Romania.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-16) At the [2021 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Romanian_census "2021 Romanian census"), the city-proper had a population of 271,692, its [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_metropolitan_area "Iași metropolitan area") had a population of 423,154,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-RPL2021-5) whereas more than 500,000 people live within its [peri-urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peri-urbanisation "Peri-urbanisation").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-INSSER-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-periurban-18) Counting 500,668 residents (as of 2018), the Iași [urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larger_urban_zone "Larger urban zone") is the second most populous in Romania after [Bucharest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest "Bucharest").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-eurostat-19) Official demographic data show that the Iași metropolitan area had surpassed 613,000 residents by 2025.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-INSSE_Domiciliu-20)

Home to the [oldest Romanian university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ia%C8%99i "University of Iași") and to the [first engineering school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gheorghe_Asachi_Technical_University_of_Ia%C8%99i "Gheorghe Asachi Technical University of Iași"), Iași is the third most important education and research centre of the country, accommodating over 60,000 students in five public universities.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-pidpc-22) The social and cultural life revolves around the [Vasile Alecsandri National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_National_Theatre "Iași National Theatre") (the oldest in Romania), the [Moldova State Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_%22Moldova%22_Philharmonic_Orchestra "Iași \"Moldova\" Philharmonic Orchestra"), the [Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C5%9Fi_Romanian_National_Opera "Iaşi Romanian National Opera"), the [Iași Athenaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_Athenaeum "Iași Athenaeum"), the [Botanical Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_Botanical_Garden "Iași Botanical Garden") (the oldest and largest in Romania), the [Central University Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_University_Library_of_Ia%C5%9Fi "Central University Library of Iaşi") (the oldest in Romania), the cultural centres and festivals, an array of museums, memorial houses, religious and historical monuments. The city is also known as the site of the largest Romanian pilgrimage which takes place every year, in October.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-pilgrim-23)

## Etymology and names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology and names")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Romania_2L_1871_telegraph_stamp_used_Jassy.JPG/250px-Romania_2L_1871_telegraph_stamp_used_Jassy.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Romania_2L_1871_telegraph_stamp_used_Jassy.JPG)

An 1871 Romanian [telegraph stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraph_stamp "Telegraph stamp"), using the historic name of _Jassy_

Scholars have different theories on the origin of the name _Iași_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-24) Some argue that the name originates with the [Sarmatian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarmatians "Sarmatians") tribe [Iazyges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iazyges "Iazyges") (of Iranian origin), one mentioned by [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid "Ovid") as _"ipse vides, onerata ferox ut ducat **Iazyx**/ per medias Histri plaustra bubulcus aquas"_[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-25) and _"**Iazyges** et Colchi Metereaque turba Getaque/ Danubii mediis vix prohibentur aquis"_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-26)

Other explanations show that the name originated from the Iranian [Alanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alans "Alans") tribe of **Jassi**, having the same origin with the Yazyges tribes [Jassic people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jassic_people "Jassic people"). In medieval times the Prut river was known as _Alanus fluvius_ and the city as _Forum Philistinorum_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-29) From this population derived the plural of the town name, _Iașii_.

Another historian wrote that the **Iasians** lived among the [Cumans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumans "Cumans") and that they left the Caucasus after the first Mongolian campaign in the West, settling temporarily near the Prut. He asserts that the ethnic name of Jasz which is given to the Iasians by the Hungarians has been erroneously identified with the Jazyges; also he shows that the word _jasz_ is a Slavic loan word.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-30) The Hungarian name of the city (_Jászvásár_) literally means 'Jassic Market'; the antiquated Romanian name, _Târgul Ieșilor_ (and the once-favoured _Iașii_), and the German _Jassenmarkt_, may indicate the same meaning.

### Ancient times

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Ancient times")]

Archaeological investigations attest to the presence of human communities on the present territory of the city and around it as far back as the prehistoric age.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Mono-31) Later settlements included those of the [Cucuteni–Trypillia culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cucuteni%E2%80%93Trypillia_culture "Cucuteni–Trypillia culture"), a late [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic")[archaeological culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeological_culture "Archaeological culture").

There is archaeological evidence of human settlements in the area of Iași dating from the 6th to 7th centuries (Curtea Domnească) and 7th to 10th centuries; these settlements contained rectangular houses with semicircular ovens.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-32) Also, many of the vessels (9th–11th centuries) found in Iași had a cross, potentially indicating that the inhabitants were Christians.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-33)

### Early development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Early development")]

In 1396, Iași is mentioned by the German crusader [Johann Schiltberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Schiltberger "Johann Schiltberger") (a participant in the [Battle of Nicopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nicopolis "Battle of Nicopolis")).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-34) The name of the city is first found in an official document in 1408. This is a grant of certain commercial privileges by the Moldavian [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Moldavian_rulers "List of Moldavian rulers")[Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Moldavia "Alexander I of Moldavia") to the Polish merchants of [Lvov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv "Lviv"). However, as buildings older than 1408 still exist, e.g. the Armenian Church believed to be originally built in 1395, it is certain that the city existed before its first surviving written mention.

### Capital of Moldavia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Capital of Moldavia")]

Around 1564, Prince [Alexandru Lăpușneanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_L%C4%83pu%C5%9Fneanu "Alexandru Lăpuşneanu") moved the Moldavian capital from [Suceava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suceava "Suceava") to Iași. Between 1561 and 1563, a school and a [Lutheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") church were founded by the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") adventurer prince, [Ioan Iacob Heraclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioan_Iacob_Heraclid "Ioan Iacob Heraclid").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-35)

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Iassy-1701.jpg/250px-Iassy-1701.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iassy-1701.jpg)

Iași in the 1700s

In 1640, [Vasile Lupu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Lupu "Vasile Lupu") established the first school in which the Romanian replaced Greek, and set up a printing press in the [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_architecture "Byzantine architecture")[Trei Ierarhi Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery "Trei Ierarhi Monastery") (_Monastery of the [Three Hierarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three\_Holy\_Hierarchs "Three Holy Hierarchs")_; built 1635–39). Between 15 September – 27 October 1642, the city hosted the [Synod of Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod_of_Ia%C8%99i "Synod of Iași") (also referred to as the Synod of Jassy).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-McGuckin2010-36) In 1643, the first volume ever printed in [Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia "Moldavia") was published in Iași.

The city was often burned down and looted by the [Tatars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nogais "Nogais") (in 1513, 1574, 1577, 1593), by the [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks") in 1538, the [Cossacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossacks "Cossacks") and Tartars (1650), or the [Poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") (1620, 1686).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-foc-37) In 1734, it was hit by the [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague"). The city was also affected by famine (1575, 1724, 1739–1740), or large local fires (1725, 1735, 1753, 1766, 1785), propagated by many buildings that were built on wooden structures.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-foc-37)

It was through the [Treaty of Jassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Jassy "Treaty of Jassy") that the sixth [Russo-Turkish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War,_1787-1792 "Russo-Turkish War, 1787-1792") was brought to a close in 1792. A Greek revolutionary manoeuvre and occupation under [Alexander Ypsilanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ypsilantis_(1792%E2%80%931828) "Alexander Ypsilantis (1792–1828)") (Αλέξανδρος Υψηλάντης) and the [Filiki Eteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filiki_Eteria "Filiki Eteria") (Φιλική Εταιρία) (1821, at the beginning of the [Greek War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_War_of_Independence "Greek War of Independence")) led to the storming of the city by the Turks in 1822.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-35) In 1844 a severe fire affected much of the city.

### Mid–19th century to 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Mid–19th century to 20th century")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Statuia_lui_Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_din_Ia%C5%9Fi3.jpg/250px-Statuia_lui_Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_din_Ia%C5%9Fi3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statuia_lui_Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_din_Ia%C5%9Fi3.jpg)

Union Square

Between 1564 and 1859, the city was the capital of Moldavia; then, between 1859 and 1862, both Iași and [Bucharest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest "Bucharest") were de facto capitals of the [United Principalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Principalities "United Principalities") of Moldavia and Wallachia. In 1862, when the union of the two principalities was recognised under the name of [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Old_Kingdom "Romanian Old Kingdom"), the national capital was established in Bucharest. For the loss caused to the city in 1861 by the removal of the seat of government to Bucharest the [constituent assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituent_Assembly "Constituent Assembly") voted 148,150 [lei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_leu "Romanian leu") to be paid in ten annual instalments, but no payment was ever made.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-35)

During [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), Iași was the capital of a much reduced Romania for two years, following the [Central Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Powers "Central Powers")' occupation of Bucharest on 6 December 1916. The capital was returned to Bucharest after the defeat of [Imperial Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Germany "Imperial Germany") and its allies in November 1918. In November–December 1918 Iași hosted the [Jassy Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jassy_Conference "Jassy Conference").

### Jewish community

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Jewish community")]

See also: [History of the Jews in Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Romania "History of the Jews in Romania")

Iași also figures prominently in [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jew "Jew") history, with the first documented presence of [Sephardi Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardi_Jews "Sephardi Jews") from the late 16th century. The oldest tomb inscription in the local cemetery probably dates to 1610.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-yivo-38) By the mid-19th century, owing to widespread [Russian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_the_Soviet_Union "History of the Jews in the Soviet Union") and [Galician Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Poland "History of the Jews in Poland")[immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration") into Moldavia, the city was at least one-third Jewish, growing to 50% Jewish by 1899 according to the _Great Geographic Dictionary of Romania_ cited by [JewishGen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JewishGen "JewishGen").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-39) The [Podu Roș Synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pod_Ro%C8%99u_Synagogue "Pod Roșu Synagogue") was built in Iași, circa 1810, by [Avraham Yehoshua Heshel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avraham_Yehoshua_Heshel "Avraham Yehoshua Heshel") of [Apta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apta_(Hasidic_dynasty) "Apta (Hasidic dynasty)"), but the synagogue became mostly [Misnagdic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misnagdim "Misnagdim") not long thereafter.

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Sinagoga_Mare_Iasi_Dec_2015.jpg/250px-Sinagoga_Mare_Iasi_Dec_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sinagoga_Mare_Iasi_Dec_2015.jpg)

[Great Synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Synagogue_(Ia%C5%9Fi) "Great Synagogue (Iaşi)") (1671)

In 1855, Iași was the home of the first-ever [Yiddish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish "Yiddish")-language newspaper, _Korot Haitim_, and, in 1876, the site of what was arguably the first-ever professional [Yiddish theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish_theatre "Yiddish theatre") performance, established by [Avraham Goldfaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Goldfaden "Abraham Goldfaden"). The words of [HaTikvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HaTikvah "HaTikvah"), the national anthem of Israel, were written in Iași by [Naftali Herz Imber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naftali_Herz_Imber "Naftali Herz Imber"). Jewish musicians in Iași played an important role as preservers of Yiddish folklore, as performers and composers.

The first Zionist [Hebrew-language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") newspaper in Romania, _Emek Israel_, was published in Iași in 1882. Zionist sports clubs, student associations and discussion groups were established in the city, most of which later merged into the [Organizația Sionistă](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Zionist_Organization "World Zionist Organization"). The Hachshara Farms in Iași were a type of training farms to prepare young people for resettlement in the Palestine region.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-40)

According to the 1930 census, with a population of 34,662 (some 34% of the city's population), Jews were the second largest ethnic group in Iași. There were over 127 [synagogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synagogue "Synagogue"). During WWII Romanian government forces under Marshall [Ion Antonescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Antonescu "Ion Antonescu") launched the [Iași pogrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_pogrom "Iași pogrom") against the city's Jewish community, which lasted from 28 June to 30 June 1941. According to Romanian authorities,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-41) over 13,266 people,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Iasipogrom2-42) or one third of the Jewish population, were massacred and many were deported. It was one of the worst pogroms during World War II.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-43) After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), in 1947, there were about 38,000 Jews living in Iași. Because of massive emigration to Israel, in 1975 there were about 3,000 Jews living in Iași and four synagogues were active.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-yivo-38)

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Gesher_edom_shul.jpg/250px-Gesher_edom_shul.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gesher_edom_shul.jpg)

Podu Roș Synagogue (photo circa 1910)

Currently, Iași has a dwindling Jewish population of ca. 300 to 600 members and two working synagogues, one of which, the 1671 [Great Synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Synagogue_(Ia%C5%9Fi) "Great Synagogue (Iaşi)"), is the [oldest surviving synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldest_synagogues_in_the_world "Oldest synagogues in the world") in Romania and among the oldest synagogues still active in Europe. A 10-year restoration project funded by UNESCO, the Romanian Ministry of Culture and the local authorities of Iași restored it to its former glory, opening in time for [Hanukkah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanukkah "Hanukkah") on 4 December 2018.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-45)

### Greek community

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Greek community")]

The history of the city and its development is marked by the thriving commercial community of [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks_in_Romania "Greeks in Romania"), as well as their occupation of public positions.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) The Greek-born [monarchs of Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_monarchs_of_Moldavia "List of monarchs of Moldavia"), politicians, teachers, clergy, doctors, philosophers, and writers contributed decisively to the emergence of Iași as an intellectual center.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46)

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Casa_Bals-Sturza11.jpg/250px-Casa_Bals-Sturza11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Casa_Bals-Sturza11.jpg)

Memorial inscription placed on the facade of the house of Greek scholar [Daniel Philippidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Philippidis "Daniel Philippidis") in Iași (address: Strada Cuza Vodă 3)

The Greek Hegemonic School (Ελληνική Ηγεμονική Σχολή) was founded in 1709 in Iași and organized in 1710 by prince [Nicholas Mavrocordatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Mavrocordatos "Nicholas Mavrocordatos").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) The city already had a Greek printing shop next to the [Trei Ierarhi Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery "Trei Ierarhi Monastery"), since the time of the ruler [Vasile Lupu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Lupu "Vasile Lupu").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) From 1774 the school was transformed into an academy with a philological, theological, mathematical and physical department, an academy that became known for its great Greek professors.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) A Greek Mechanical School also operated in Iași at the same time.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) From 1728, the [Greek language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") began to be taught as a subject in the existing school, and from 1776 it was established as the language for all subjects at the school.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46)

Iași was an important center of the [revolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary "Revolutionary") organization _[Filiki Eteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filiki\_Eteria "Filiki Eteria")_ and was chosen as the core of the formation of the Greek forces.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) Here [Georgios Lassanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgios_Lassanis "Georgios Lassanis") from [Kozani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozani "Kozani") gathered and recruited warriors on the orders of [Alexander Ypsilantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ypsilantis "Alexander Ypsilantis").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) On 24 February 1821, Alexander Ypsilantis issued a proclamation at Trei Ierarhi Monastery and at the head of approximately 200 infantry and cavalry, declared the [Greek Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_War_of_Independence "Greek War of Independence").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-47) The struggle for the liberation of [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Hellenic_Republic "First Hellenic Republic") began in Iași.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46)

The modern "Greek Community of Iași" was founded in 1990.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) The community has approximately 400 official members but the Greeks in Iași are much more numerous according to its president Marika Pieptou.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) At the end of May 2008, the 7th Greek Language "[Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiad "Olympiad")" was organized in the city of Iași, in the halls of the “Ion Simionescu” General School.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) 66 students of Greek origin and [philhellenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philhellenism "Philhellenism"), of all ages and language levels, took part in the competition.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) The organizers were honored with the presence of the Minister of Education of Romania, Anghel Stanciu, the Chairman of the Education Committee of the Romanian Parliament, as well as representatives of the local authorities and the presidency of the [Hellenic Union of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Union_of_Romania "Hellenic Union of Romania").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46) Also, at the [Alexandru Ioan Cuza University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_University "Alexandru Ioan Cuza University") there is a department (lectorate) of Greek language.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-unicrete-46)

### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: World War II")]

Main article: [Iași pogrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_pogrom "Iași pogrom")

During the war, while the full scale of [the Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust") remained generally unknown to the [Allied Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II"), the [Iași pogrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C5%9Fi_pogrom "Iaşi pogrom"), launched by the Romanian dictator, [Ion Antonescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Antonescu "Ion Antonescu"), stood as one of the well-known examples of brutality toward the Jews. The pogrom lasted from 29 June to 6 July 1941, and over 13,266 people,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Iasipogrom-48) or one third of the Jewish population, were massacred in the pogrom itself or in its aftermath, and many were deported. Particularly brutal was the massacre of Jews who were forced on sealed trains in the brutal summer heat. Over half of the occupants perished in these trains, which were aimlessly driven throughout the countryside with no particular destination.

Main articles: [First Jassy–Kishinev Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Jassy%E2%80%93Kishinev_Offensive "First Jassy–Kishinev Offensive") and [Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Jassy%E2%80%93Kishinev_Offensive "Second Jassy–Kishinev Offensive")

In May 1944, the Iași area became the scene of ferocious fighting between Romanian-[German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") forces and the advancing [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union")[Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army") and the city was partially destroyed. The German [Panzergrenadier Division _Großdeutschland_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grossdeutschland_Division "Grossdeutschland Division") won a defensive victory at the [Battle of Târgu Frumos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_T%C3%A2rgu_Frumos "First Battle of Târgu Frumos"), near Iași, which was the object of several [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO") studies during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"). By 20 August, Iași had been taken by Soviet forces.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-49)

Iași suffered heavy damage due to Soviet (June–July 1941, June 1944) and American (June 1944) airstrikes, respectively. The bombing of Soviet aviation and artillery on 20 August 1944, resulted in more than 5,000 civilian deaths and the destruction of two-thirds of the city.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-50)

### Post-World War II era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Post-World War II era")]

Iași experienced a major wave of industrialisation, in 1955–1989.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-monumente-51) During this period of time, it received numerous migrants from rural regions, and the urban area expanded.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-52) In the [Communist era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Romania "Socialist Republic of Romania"), Iași saw a growth of 235% in population and 69% in area. The local systematisation plans of the old city started in 1960 and continued in the 1970s and 1980s as part of the larger national [systematisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systematization_(Romania) "Systematization (Romania)") programme; however, the urban planning was sometimes arbitrary and followed by dysfunctions.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Spatial_Evolution_Ia%C8%99i_Stoleriu_and_Stoleriu-53) By 1989, Iași had become highly industrialised, with 108,000 employees (representing 47% of the total workforce) active in 46 large [state-owned enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-owned_enterprise "State-owned enterprise"), in various industries: machine building and heavy equipment, chemical, textile, pharmaceutical, metallurgical, electronics, food, energy, building materials, furniture.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-industria-55)

After [the end of the Communist regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Revolution "Romanian Revolution") and the transition to a free market economy, the private sector has grown steadily, while much of the old industry (such as the industrial sector) gradually decayed.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Geography")]

### Topography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Topography")]

See also: [Seven hills of Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_hills_of_Ia%C8%99i "Seven hills of Iași")

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/RO_IS_Ia%C5%9Fi_%2C_panoramic_view_4.JPG/250px-RO_IS_Ia%C5%9Fi_%2C_panoramic_view_4.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RO_IS_Ia%C5%9Fi_,_panoramic_view_4.JPG)

Panoramic view of the Copou Hill

Located in northeastern Romania, at the contact between the [Jijia Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jijia_Plain "Jijia Plain") and the [Bârlad Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A2rlad_Plateau "Bârlad Plateau"), Iași used to be the crossroads place of the historic trade routes that passed through Moldavia coming from the [Kingdom of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth"), [Habsburg monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy"), [Tsardom of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia "Tsardom of Russia"), and [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople").

The city lies on the [Bahlui River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahlui_River "Bahlui River") valley, a tributary of the [Jijia River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jijia_River_(Prut) "Jijia River (Prut)") (tributary of the [Prut River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prut_River "Prut River")). The surrounding country is one of uplands and woods, featuring monasteries and parks. Iași itself stands amid vineyards and gardens, partly on hills, partly in the in-between valley.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChisholm1911-35)

The central part of the city is located on the 25 m (82[ft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_(unit) "Foot (unit)")) fluvial terrace of the Bahlui River (the so-called Palat Terrace).[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-56) From this nucleus, the city evolved after the medieval times toward south and north on the Bahlui River floodplain and on the adjacent hills. The southern part of the city lies on the [Iași Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_Ridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Iași Ridge (page does not exist)") ([Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"): _Coasta Iașilor_) (the northernmost hill of the Bârlad Plateau). Considering the present day extension of the administrative boundaries, the city territory has an altitudinal extension of 320 m (1,050 ft), between the 34.5 [m a.s.l.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metres_above_sea_level "Metres above sea level") (113.19 ft) in the Bahlui River floodplain, at the Holboca bridge, and 354.77 m a.s.l. (1,163.94 ft), at the edge of the [Repedea Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repedea_Hill_Fossil_Site "Repedea Hill Fossil Site").

It is a common belief that Iași is built on seven hills ([Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"): _coline_): Breazu, Bucium, Cetățuia, Copou, Galata, Repedea and Șorogari, thus triggering comparisons with [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Climate")]

Under the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Iaşi falls within either a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (_Dfa_, near _Dfb_) if the 0°C (32°F) isotherm is used, or a [humid temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_temperate_climate "Humid temperate climate") (_Cfa_) bordering on an [oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") (_Cfb_) if the −3°C (27°F) isotherm is used. Iași experiences four distinct seasons. Summers are warm with temperatures sometimes exceeding 35°C (95°F) while winters are cold and windy with moderate snowfall and temperatures at night sometimes dropping below −15°C (5°F).

## Cityscape

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Cityscape")]

### Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Architecture")]

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Pia%C8%9Ba_Palat%2C_Ia%C8%99i%2C_Roumanie.jpg/250px-Pia%C8%9Ba_Palat%2C_Ia%C8%99i%2C_Roumanie.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pia%C8%9Ba_Palat,_Ia%C8%99i,_Roumanie.jpg)

The neo-Gothic [Palace of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Culture_(Ia%C8%99i) "Palace of Culture (Iași)"), built on the old ruins of the mediaeval Princely Court is a reconstruction of the former neoclassical Princely Palace of Moldavia

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Hotel_Traian%2C_Ia%C8%99i.JPG/250px-Hotel_Traian%2C_Ia%C8%99i.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hotel_Traian,_Ia%C8%99i.JPG)

Grand Hotel Traian (Union Square), designed and built by [Gustave Eiffel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Eiffel "Gustave Eiffel")

Iași features historical monuments, 500-year-old churches and monasteries, contemporary architecture, many of them listed on the [National Register of Historic Monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Monuments_in_Romania "National Register of Historic Monuments in Romania"). Notable architecture includes the [Trei Ierarhi Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery "Trei Ierarhi Monastery"), part of the [tentative list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Romania "List of World Heritage Sites in Romania") of [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site"), or the neo-Gothic [Palace of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Culture_(Ia%C5%9Fi) "Palace of Culture (Iaşi)"), built on the old ruins of the mediaeval Princely Court of Moldavia.

During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and the [Communist era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Romania "Communist Romania") many historical buildings in the old city centre (around Union Square area) were destroyed or demolished, and replaced by [International style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_style_(architecture) "International style (architecture)") buildings and also a new mainly [Mid-Century modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-Century_modern "Mid-Century modern") style [Civic Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic_Centre "Civic Centre") was built around the Old Market Square (The Central Hall).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-monumente-51)

The mid-1990s to early-2000s brought the first non-industrial glass [curtain walled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtain_wall_(architecture) "Curtain wall (architecture)") buildings (Romtelecom, Hotel Europa), while in 2012, in close proximity to the Palace of Culture, the [Palas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palas_Ia%C8%99i "Palas Iași") shopping mall and office complex was inaugurated.

Other significant buildings include:

*   [Alexandru Ioan Cuza University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_University "Alexandru Ioan Cuza University") main building (1897), a mixture of the [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") and [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture "Baroque architecture") styles, houses the famous _Hall of the Lost Footsteps_ where one can admire the works of the painter [Sabin Bălașa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabin_B%C4%83la%C5%9Fa "Sabin Bălaşa");
*   ["Vasile Alecsandri" National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C5%9Fi_National_Theatre "Iaşi National Theatre"), built between 1894 and 1896 in Neoclassic style with Baroque and [Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo "Rococo") inspired painted and sculpted ornaments;
*   [Dosoftei House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dosoftei_House?action=edit&redlink=1 "Dosoftei House (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa%20Dosoftei "ro:Casa Dosoftei")], a building from the second half of the 17th century in which in 1679, the metropolitan bishop Dosoftei settled the second typography in Moldavia. With three façades, arched and right-angled windows, the edifice was restored between 1966 and 1969. It houses the department of old literature of the Romanian Literature Museum;
*   [Roznovanu Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roznovanu_Palace "Roznovanu Palace") (The City Hall), second half of the 18th century, rebuilt between 1830 and 1833, it hosted the Romanian government during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I");
*   [Union Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Union Museum (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzeul%20Unirii%20din%20Ia%C8%99i "ro:Muzeul Unirii din Iași")], 1806, [Empire style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_style "Empire style"), the palace served as the royal residence of [Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza "Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza") between 1859 and 1862 and in 1917–1918, during World War I, as the royal residence of king [Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_of_Romania "Ferdinand of Romania");
*   [Pogor House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pogor_House?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pogor House (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casa%20Memorial%C4%83%20%E2%80%9EVasile%20Pogor%E2%80%9D "ro:Casa Memorială „Vasile Pogor”")], 1850, a meeting place for the city intellectuals, the headquarters of Literary Society [Junimea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junimea "Junimea") (1863) and of the [Convorbiri Literare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convorbiri_Literare "Convorbiri Literare") (Literary Interlocutions) magazine (1867), houses the Romanian Literature Museum;
*   [Luceafărul Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luceaf%C4%83rul_Theatre_(Ia%C8%99i) "Luceafărul Theatre (Iași)"), 1987, a unique modern building in Romania;
*   [Central University Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_University_Library_of_Ia%C5%9Fi "Central University Library of Iaşi"), 1934, incorporates [Greek Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Revival_architecture "Greek Revival architecture") elements;
*   [Great Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C5%9Fi_railway_station "Iaşi railway station"), 1870, inspired by the Venetian [Doge's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doge's_Palace,_Venice "Doge's Palace, Venice").

### Religious buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Religious buildings")]

See also: [List of churches in Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_churches_in_Ia%C8%99i "List of churches in Iași")

Iași is the seat of the [Romanian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Orthodox_Church "Romanian Orthodox Church")[Metropolitan of Moldavia and Bukovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolis_of_Moldavia_and_Bukovina "Metropolis of Moldavia and Bukovina"), and of the [Roman Catholic Bishop of Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Ia%C8%99i "Roman Catholic Diocese of Iași"). The city and the surrounding area house more than 10 monasteries and 100 historical churches.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Pilgrimage-62) Among the oldest is [Princely Saint Nicholas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_Saint_Nicholas_Church "Princely Saint Nicholas Church") (1491), dating from the reign of [Stephen the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_the_Great "Stephen the Great"), and the [Metropolitan Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Cathedral,_Ia%C8%99i "Metropolitan Cathedral, Iași") is the largest of its kind in Romania. The [Trei Ierarhi Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery "Trei Ierarhi Monastery"), a unique monument, considered to be an architectural masterpiece,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-63) was erected in 1635–1639 by Vasile Lupu, and adorned with gilded carvings on its outer walls and twin towers.

*   [Metropolitan Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Cathedral,_Ia%C8%99i "Metropolitan Cathedral, Iași") (1839/1886), the largest [Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Orthodox_Church "Romanian Orthodox Church") church in Romania, a late [Renaissance style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture "Renaissance architecture"), with Baroque elements and [Gheorghe Tattarescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gheorghe_Tattarescu "Gheorghe Tattarescu") paintings, it contains the relics of Saint Paracheva (sometimes known colloquially in English as Saint Friday);[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Pilgrimage-62)
*   [Golia Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golia_Monastery "Golia Monastery"), 1564, rebuilt in 1650 in late-Renaissance style with Byzantine frescoes and intricately carved doorways, is a monumental construction, a monastery in the middle of the city, surrounded by tall walls, with corner turrets, and a 30 m (98.43[ft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_(unit) "Foot (unit)")) height bell tower;
*   [Old Catholic Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assumption_of_Mary_Church,_Ia%C8%99i "Assumption of Mary Church, Iași"), 1782, in Baroque style, and [New Catholic Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_Queen_of_Ia%C8%99i_Cathedral "Our Lady Queen of Iași Cathedral"), 2005;
*   [Armenian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Church,_Ia%C8%99i "Armenian Church, Iași"), built in 1395, testifies the existence of an important Armenian community in these parts of Romania;
*   [Great Synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Synagogue_(Ia%C8%99i) "Great Synagogue (Iași)"), in late Baroque style, built in 1657–1671, is the [oldest surviving synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldest_synagogues_in_the_World "Oldest synagogues in the World") in Romania and one of the oldest in Europe.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-Pilgrimage-62)

#### Pilgrimage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Pilgrimage")]

The city has become a major Christian pilgrimage site since the [early modern period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_period "Early modern period"). In 1641, the relics of [Saint Parascheva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parascheva_of_the_Balkans "Parascheva of the Balkans") were brought to Iași. Each year, around 14 October, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims gather to commemorate Saint Parascheva, while the city itself established its Celebration Days at the same time.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-65) The October pilgrimage is one of the largest in Europe, drawing people all over Romania as well as from neighbouring Orthodox countries.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-pilgrim-23)

During the entire year, pilgrimages to Iași can also involve visits to a large number of religious sites, both within and around the city.

### Gardens, parks and natural landmarks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ia%C8%99i&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Gardens, parks and natural landmarks")]

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Barajul_Ciric_II.jpg/250px-Barajul_Ciric_II.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Barajul_Ciric_II.jpg)

Ciric Park

Iași has a diverse array of public spaces, from city squares to public parks.

[![Image 45](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Eminescu_copou.JPG/250px-Eminescu_copou.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eminescu_copou.JPG)

[Mihai Eminescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihai_Eminescu "Mihai Eminescu")'s statue and his Linden Tree in [Copou Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copou_Park "Copou Park")

Begun in 1833, at the time when Iași was the capital of [Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia "Moldavia"), by Prince [Mihail Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Sturdza "Mihail Sturdza") and under the plans of Gheorghe Asachi and Mihail Singurov, [Copou Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copou_Park "Copou Park") was integrated into the city and marks one of the first Romanian coordinated public parks. The oldest monument in Romania stands in the middle of the park, the [Obelisk of Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk_of_Lions?action=edit&redlink=1 "Obelisk of Lions (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obeliscul%20cu%20lei%20din%20Ia%C8%99i "ro:Obeliscul cu lei din Iași")] (1834), a 13.5 m (44.29[ft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_(unit) "Foot (unit)")) tall [obelisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelisk "Obelisk"), dedicated to the _[Regulamentul Organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulamentul\_Organic "Regulamentul Organic")_, the first law on political, administrative and juridical organisation in Romanian Principalities.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-66)

Founded in 1856, the [Botanical Garden of Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botanical_Garden_of_Ia%C5%9Fi "Botanical Garden of Iaşi"), the first botanical garden in Romania, has an area of over 100 hectares, and more than 10,000 species of plants.

[Iași Exhibition Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i_Exhibition_Park "Iași Exhibition Park") was opened in 1923 and built under the co-ordination of the architect [N. Ghica Budești](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghica_family "Ghica family").

The [Ciric Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciric_Park?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ciric Park (page does not exist)"), located in the north-eastern part of Iași, consists of parkland and four lakes.

[Eminescu's Linden Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminescu's_Linden_Tree "Eminescu's Linden Tree") ([Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"): _Teiul lui Eminescu_) is a 500-year-old silver linden (_[Tilia tomentosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilia\_tomentosa "Tilia tomentosa")[Moench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrad\_Moench "Conrad Moench")_) situated in [Copou Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copou_Park "Copou Park"). [Mihai Eminescu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihai_Eminescu "Mihai Eminescu") reportedly wrote some of his best works underneath this linden tree, rendering it one of Romania's most important [natural monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_monument "Natural monument") and a notable Iași landmark.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-67) The [Odd Poplars Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odd_Poplars_Alley?action=edit&redlink=1 "Odd Poplars Alley (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plopii%20f%C4%83r%C4%83%20so%C8%9B "ro:Plopii fără soț")], in Bucium neighbourhood, is another spot where Mihai Eminescu sought inspiration (the poem "Down Where the Lonely Poplars Grow"). In 1973, the 15 white poplars still left (with the age ranges between 233 and 371 years) were declared natural monuments.

Iași County has 387 centuries-old trees, of which 224 were declared monument trees and 160 got the [Romanian Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Academy "Romanian Academy")'s approval and are proposed for such a classification. Most of them are oak or linden trees. The oldest tree in the county is the 675-year-old hybrid linden (_[Tilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilia "Tilia")_) tree located in the courtyard of [Bârnova Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A2rnova_Monastery "Bârnova Monastery"), in the vicinity of Iași. When the linden was about 57 years old and about 14 cm (5.5 in) in diameter, Iași was mentioned as an urban settlement, during the reign of Prince [Alexander the Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Moldavia "Alexander I of Moldavia") (1408).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i#cite_note-68)
