The Franciscan Friar [William of Rubruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_of_Rubruck "William of Rubruck"), who visited the court of the Great Khan in the 1250s, listed "the Blac",[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-31) or Vlachs, among the peoples who paid tribute to the Mongols, but the Vlachs' territory is uncertain.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-FOOTNOTES%C4%83l%C4%83gean2005196-32)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpinei1986131-33) Friar William described "Blakia" as "[Assan's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asen_dynasty "Asen dynasty") territory"[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-34) south of the Lower Danube, showing that he [identified it with the northern regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_lands_across_the_Danube "Bulgarian lands across the Danube") of the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-FOOTNOTEV%C3%A1s%C3%A1ry200530-35) Later in the 14th century, King [Charles I of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_I_of_Hungary "Charles I of Hungary") attempted to expand his realm and the influence of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") eastwards after the fall of Cuman rule, and ordered a campaign under the command of [Phynta de Mende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phynta_de_Mende?action=edit&redlink=1 "Phynta de Mende (page does not exist)") (1324). In 1342 and 1345, the Hungarians were victorious in a battle against [Tatar-Mongols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars"); the conflict was resolved by the death of [Jani Beg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jani_Beg "Jani Beg"), in 1357. The Polish chronicler [Jan Długosz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_D%C5%82ugosz "Jan Długosz") mentioned Moldavians (under the name _Wallachians_) as having joined a military expedition in 1342, under King [Władysław I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C5%82adys%C5%82aw_I_the_Elbow-high "Władysław I the Elbow-high"), against the [Margraviate of Brandenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margraviate_of_Brandenburg "Margraviate of Brandenburg").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-36)

In 1353, [Dragoș](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drago%C8%99 "Dragoș"), mentioned as a Vlach _[Knyaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knyaz "Knyaz")_ in [Maramureș](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maramure%C8%99 "Maramureș"), was sent by [Louis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_I_of_Hungary "Louis I of Hungary") to establish a line of defense against the [Golden Horde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horde "Golden Horde") forces of Mongols on the [Siret River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siret_River "Siret River"). This expedition resulted in a polity vassal to Hungary, in the [Baia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baia "Baia") (_Târgul Moldovei_ or _Moldvabánya_) region.

[Bogdan of Cuhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdan_I_of_Moldavia "Bogdan I of Moldavia"), another Vlach [voivode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voivode "Voivode") from Maramureș who had fallen out with the Hungarian king, crossed the Carpathians in 1359, took control of Moldavia, and succeeded in wrenching Moldavia from Hungarian control. His realm extended north to the [Cheremosh River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheremosh_River "Cheremosh River"), while the southern part of Moldavia was still occupied by the Tatar Mongols.

After first residing in Baia, Bogdan moved Moldavia's seat to [Siret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siret "Siret") (it was to remain there until [Petru II Mușat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petru_II_of_Moldavia "Petru II of Moldavia") moved it to [Suceava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suceava "Suceava"); it was finally moved to [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași") under [Alexandru Lăpușneanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_L%C4%83pu%C8%99neanu "Alexandru Lăpușneanu") - in 1565). The area around Suceava, roughly correspondent to future [Bukovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukovina "Bukovina"), would later constitute one of the two administrative divisions of the new realm, under the name _Țara de Sus_ (the "Upper Land"), whereas the rest, on both sides of the [Prut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prut "Prut") river, formed _Țara de Jos_ (the "Lower Land").

Disfavored by the brief union of [Angevin Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Poland_during_the_Piast_dynasty "History of Poland during the Piast dynasty") and Hungary (the latter was still the country's overlord), Bogdan's successor [Lațcu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%C8%9Bcu_of_Moldavia "Lațcu of Moldavia") accepted [conversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_conversion "Religious conversion") to [Latin Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") around 1370. Despite the founding of the [Latin diocese of Siret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Siret "Roman Catholic Diocese of Siret"), this move did not have any lasting consequences. Despite remaining officially [Eastern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") and culturally connected with the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") after 1382, princes of the [House of Bogdan-Mușat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Bogdan-Mu%C8%99at "House of Bogdan-Mușat") entered a conflict with the [Constantinople Patriarchate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_Patriarch_of_Constantinople "Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople") about control of appointments to the newly founded [Moldavian Metropolitan seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_of_Moldavia "Metropolitan of Moldavia"); [Patriarch Antony IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarch_Antony_IV_of_Constantinople "Patriarch Antony IV of Constantinople") even cast an [anathema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anathema "Anathema") over Moldavia after [Roman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_I_of_Moldavia "Roman I of Moldavia") expelled Constantinople's candidate, sending him back to Byzantium. The crisis was finally settled in favor of the Moldavian princes under [Alexander I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Moldavia "Alexander I of Moldavia"). Nevertheless, religious policy remained complex: while conversions to faiths other than Orthodox were discouraged (and forbidden for princes), Moldavia included sizable Latin Catholic communities (Germans and [Magyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magyars "Magyars")), as well as [Armenians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians_in_Romania "Armenians in Romania") of the non-Chalcedonian [Armenian Apostolic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church"); after 1460, the country welcomed [Hussite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite "Hussite") refugees (founders of [Ciuburciu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciuburciu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ciuburciu (page does not exist)") and, probably, [Huși](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu%C8%99i "Huși")).

The principality of Moldavia covered the entire geographic region of Moldavia. In various periods, various other territories were politically connected with the Moldavian principality. This is the case of the province of [Pokuttya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokuttya "Pokuttya"), the fiefdoms of [Cetatea de Baltă](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cetatea_de_Balt%C4%83 "Cetatea de Baltă") and [Ciceu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciceu "Ciceu") (both in [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania")) or, at a later date, the territories between the Dniester and the Bug rivers.

Petru II profited from the end of the Hungarian-Polish union and moved the country closer to the [Jagiellonian realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Poland_during_the_Jagiellonian_dynasty "History of Poland during the Jagiellonian dynasty"), becoming a [vassal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vassalage "Vassalage") of [Władysław II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C5%82adys%C5%82aw_II_Jagie%C5%82%C5%82o "Władysław II Jagiełło") on September 26, 1387. This gesture was to have unexpected consequences: Petru supplied the Polish ruler with funds needed in the war against the [Teutonic Knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teutonic_Knights "Teutonic Knights"), and was granted control over [Pokuttya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokuttya "Pokuttya") until the debt was repaid; as this is not recorded to have been carried out, the region became disputed by the two states, until it was lost by Moldavia in the [Battle of Obertyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Obertyn "Battle of Obertyn") (1531). Prince Petru also expanded his rule southwards to the [Danube Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube_Delta "Danube Delta"). His brother Roman I conquered the Hungarian-ruled [Cetatea Albă](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi "Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi") in 1392, giving Moldavia an outlet to the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"), before being toppled from the throne for supporting [Fyodor Koriatovych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Koriatovych "Fyodor Koriatovych") in his conflict with [Vytautas the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vytautas_the_Great "Vytautas the Great") of [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania "Grand Duchy of Lithuania"). Under [Stephen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_I_of_Moldavia "Stephen I of Moldavia").

Although [Alexander I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_I_of_Moldavia "Alexander I of Moldavia") was brought to the throne in 1400 by the Hungarians (with assistance from [Mircea I of Wallachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mircea_I_of_Wallachia "Mircea I of Wallachia")), he shifted his allegiances towards Poland (notably engaging Moldavian forces on the Polish side in the [Battle of Grunwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Grunwald "Battle of Grunwald") and the [Siege of Marienburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Marienburg_(1410) "Siege of Marienburg (1410)")), and placed his own choice of rulers in Wallachia. His reign was one of the most successful in Moldavia's history, but also saw the first confrontation with the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Turks "Ottoman Turks") at Cetatea Albă in 1420, and later even a conflict with the Poles. A deep crisis was to follow Alexandru's long reign, with his successors battling each other in a succession of wars that divided the country until the murder of [Bogdan II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdan_II_of_Moldavia "Bogdan II of Moldavia") and the ascension of [Petru III Aron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_III_Aaron "Peter III Aaron") in 1451. Nevertheless, Moldavia was subject to further Hungarian interventions after that moment, as [Matthias Corvinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Corvinus "Matthias Corvinus") deposed Aron and backed [Alexăndrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex%C4%83ndrel "Alexăndrel") to the throne in [Suceava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suceava "Suceava"). Petru Aron's rule also signified the beginning of Moldavia's [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") allegiance, as the ruler agreed to pay [tribute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute "Tribute") to Sultan [Mehmed II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmed_II "Mehmed II").

### Late Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Late Middle Ages")]

Main article: [Stephen the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_the_Great "Stephen the Great")

See also: [Moldavian–Ottoman Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian%E2%80%93Ottoman_Wars "Moldavian–Ottoman Wars")

Under [Stephen the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_III_of_Moldavia "Stephen III of Moldavia"), who took the throne and subsequently came to an agreement with [Casimir IV of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazimierz_IV_Jagiellon "Kazimierz IV Jagiellon") in 1457, the state reached its most glorious period. Stephen blocked Hungarian interventions in the [Battle of Baia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baia "Battle of Baia"), invaded Wallachia in 1471, and dealt with Ottoman reprisals in a major victory (the 1475 [Battle of Vaslui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vaslui "Battle of Vaslui")); after feeling threatened by Polish ambitions, he also attacked [Galicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galicia_(Eastern_Europe) "Galicia (Eastern Europe)") and resisted [a Polish invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_Campaign_(1497%E2%80%931499) "Moldavian Campaign (1497–1499)") in the [Battle of the Cosmin Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Cosmin_Forest "Battle of the Cosmin Forest") (1497). However, he had to surrender [Chilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiliia "Kiliia") (now Kiliia) and [Cetatea Albă](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi "Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi") (now Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi), the two main fortresses in the [Budjak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budjak "Budjak"), to the Ottomans in 1484, and in 1498 he had to accept Ottoman suzerainty, when he was forced to agree to continue paying tribute to Sultan [Bayezid II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayezid_II "Bayezid II"). Following the taking of [Hotin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khotyn "Khotyn") (Khotyn) and [Pokuttya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokuttya "Pokuttya"), Stephen's rule also brought a brief extension of Moldavian rule into [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania"): Cetatea de Baltă and [Ciceu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciceu "Ciceu") became his [fiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiefdom "Fiefdom") in 1489.

### Early Modern Era and Renaissance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Early Modern Era and Renaissance")]

Main article: [Early Modern Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Romania "Early Modern Romania")

See also: [Early Modern Wallachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Wallachia "Early Modern Wallachia") and [Early Modern Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Modern_Transylvania "Early Modern Transylvania")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Khotyn_3.jpg/250px-Khotyn_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Khotyn_3.jpg)

[Khotyn Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khotyn_Fortress "Khotyn Fortress") on the [Dniester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dniester "Dniester") River, present-day [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"), then bordering the northern frontier of the Moldavian Principality and southern [Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth")

Under [Bogdan III the One-Eyed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogdan_III_the_One-Eyed "Bogdan III the One-Eyed"), Ottoman overlordship was confirmed in the shape that would rapidly evolve into control over Moldavia's affairs. [Peter IV Rareș](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_IV_Rare%C8%99 "Peter IV Rareș"), who reigned in the 1530s and 1540s, clashed with the [Habsburg monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") over his ambitions in Transylvania (losing possessions in the region to [George Martinuzzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Martinuzzi "George Martinuzzi")), was defeated in Pokuttya by Poland, and failed in his attempt to extricate Moldavia from Ottoman rule – the country lost [Bender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bender,_Moldova "Bender, Moldova") to the Ottomans, who included it in their [Silistra Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silistra_Eyalet "Silistra Eyalet").

A period of profound crisis followed. Moldavia stopped issuing its own coinage c.1520, under [Prince Ștefăniță](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_IV_of_Moldavia "Stephen IV of Moldavia"), when it was confronted with rapid depletion of funds and rising demands from the [Porte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Porte "Ottoman Porte"). Such problems became endemic when the country, brought into the [Great Turkish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Turkish_War "Great Turkish War"), suffered the impact of the [stagnation of the Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagnation_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "Stagnation of the Ottoman Empire"); at one point, during the 1650s and 1660s, princes began relying on [counterfeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterfeit "Counterfeit") coinage (usually copies of [Swedish riksdalers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_riksdaler "Swedish riksdaler"), as was that issued by [Eustratie Dabija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustratie_Dabija "Eustratie Dabija")). The economic decline was accompanied by a failure to maintain state structures: the [feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism")-based [Moldavian military forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_military_forces "Moldavian military forces") were no longer convoked, and the few troops maintained by the rulers remained professional [mercenaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary "Mercenary") such as the _[seimeni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seimeni "Seimeni")_.

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Jassy_%28Iasi%29-Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery_%28J.Rey%2C_1845%29.jpg/250px-Jassy_%28Iasi%29-Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery_%28J.Rey%2C_1845%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jassy_(Iasi)-Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery_(J.Rey,_1845).jpg)

[Trei Ierarhi Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trei_Ierarhi_Monastery "Trei Ierarhi Monastery") in Iași, housed the [Vasilian College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilian_College "Vasilian College"), an institution of higher learning founded in 1640

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Moldavia%2C_Transylvania_and_Wallachia_under_Michael_the_Brave%27s_authority_%281600%29.png/250px-Moldavia%2C_Transylvania_and_Wallachia_under_Michael_the_Brave%27s_authority_%281600%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mihai_1600.png)

In 1600, [Michael the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_the_Brave "Michael the Brave") became Prince of Wallachia, of Transylvania, and of Moldavia.

However, Moldavia and the similarly affected Wallachia remained both important sources of income for the Ottoman Empire and relatively prosperous agricultural economies (especially as suppliers of grain and cattle – the latter was especially relevant in Moldavia, which remained an under-populated country of [pastures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasture "Pasture")). In time, much of the resources were tied to the [Ottoman economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "Economic history of the Ottoman Empire"), either through [monopolies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") on trade that were only lifted in 1829, after the [Treaty of Adrianople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Adrianople_(1829) "Treaty of Adrianople (1829)") (which did not affect all domains directly), or through the raise in direct taxes - the one demanded by the Ottomans from the princes, as well as the ones demanded by the princes from the country's population. Taxes were directly proportional with Ottoman requests, but also with the growing importance of Ottoman appointment and sanctioning of princes in front of election by the [boyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyar "Boyar") and the boyar Council – _[Sfatul boieresc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sfatul\_boieresc?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sfatul boieresc (page does not exist)")[[ro](https://ro.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sfatul%20domnesc "ro:Sfatul domnesc")]_ (drawing in a competition among pretenders, which also implied the intervention of creditors as suppliers of bribes). The fiscal system soon included taxes such as the _[văcărit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical\_Romanian\_taxes "Historical Romanian taxes")_ (a tax on head of cattle), first introduced by [Iancu Sasul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iancu_Sasul "Iancu Sasul") in the 1580s.

The economic opportunities offered brought about a significant influx of [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks_in_Romania "Greeks in Romania") and [Levantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") financiers and officials, who entered a stiff competition with the high boyars over appointments to the Court. As the [manor system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manorialism "Manorialism") suffered the blows of economic crises, and in the absence of [salarisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salary "Salary") (which implied that persons in office could decide their own income), obtaining princely appointment became the major focus of a boyar's career. Such changes also implied the decline of free peasantry and the rise of [serfdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serfdom "Serfdom"), as well as the rapid fall in the importance of low boyars (a traditional institution, the latter soon became marginal, and, in more successful instances, added to the population of towns); however, they also implied a rapid transition towards a [monetary economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_economy "Monetary economy"), based on exchanges in foreign currency. Serfdom was doubled by the much less numerous slave population (_robi_), composed of migrant [Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma_in_Romania "Roma in Romania") and captured [Nogais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nogais "Nogais").

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Partitions_of_Moldavia.jpg/250px-Partitions_of_Moldavia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Partitions_of_Moldavia.jpg)

Moldavia through the ages

The conflict between princes and boyars was to become exceptionally violent – the latter group, who frequently appealed to the Ottoman court in order to have princes comply with its demands, was persecuted by rulers such as [Alexandru Lăpușneanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_L%C4%83pu%C8%99neanu "Alexandru Lăpușneanu") and [John III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_III_the_Terrible "John III the Terrible"). Ioan Vodă's revolt against the Ottomans ended in his execution (1574). The country descended into political chaos, with frequent Ottoman and [Tatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars") incursions and pillages. The claims of Mușatins to the crown and the traditional system of succession were ended by scores of illegitimate reigns; one of the usurpers, [Ioan Iacob Heraclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioan_Iacob_Heraclid "Ioan Iacob Heraclid"), was a [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") Greek who encouraged the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") and attempted to introduce [Lutheranism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") to Moldavia.

In 1595, the rise of the [Movilești](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movile%C8%99ti "Movilești") boyars to the throne with [Ieremia Movilă](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ieremia_Movil%C4%83 "Ieremia Movilă") coincided with the start of frequent anti-Ottoman and anti-[Habsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") military expeditions of the [Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth") into Moldavian territory (see _[Moldavian Magnate Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian\_Magnate\_Wars "Moldavian Magnate Wars")_), and rivalries between pretenders to the Moldavian throne encouraged by the three competing powers.

The Wallachian prince [Michael the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_the_Brave "Michael the Brave"), after previously taking over [Transylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania"), also deposed Prince Ieremia Movilă, in 1600, and managed to become the first Prince to rule over Moldavia, Wallachia, and Transylvania;[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-37)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-White2000-38)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-39) the episode ended in Polish conquests of lands down to [Bucharest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest "Bucharest"), soon ended by the outbreak of the [Polish–Swedish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Swedish_War_(1600%E2%80%931611) "Polish–Swedish War (1600–1611)") and the reestablishment of Ottoman rule. Polish incursions were dealt a blow by the Ottomans.

During the 1620 [Battle of Cecora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cecora_(1620) "Battle of Cecora (1620)"), the voivode of the Principality of Moldavia, was assassinated by the [Septilici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septilici_family "Septilici family") noble family in which also saw an end to the reign of [Gaspar Graziani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspar_Graziani "Gaspar Graziani").

A period of relative peace followed during the more prosperous and prestigious rule of [Vasile Lupu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasile_Lupu "Vasile Lupu"). He took the throne as a boyar appointee in 1637 and began battling his rival [Gheorghe Ștefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gheorghe_%C8%98tefan "Gheorghe Ștefan"), as well as the Wallachian prince [Matei Basarab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matei_Basarab "Matei Basarab"). However, his invasion of Wallachia, with the backing of [Cossack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack")[Hetman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hetmans_of_Ukrainian_Cossacks "Hetmans of Ukrainian Cossacks")[Bohdan Khmelnytsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohdan_Khmelnytsky "Bohdan Khmelnytsky"), ended in disaster at the [Battle of Finta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Finta "Battle of Finta") in 1653. A few years later, Moldavia was occupied for two short intervals by the anti-Ottoman Wallachian prince [Constantin Șerban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantin_%C8%98erban "Constantin Șerban"), who clashed with the first ruler of the [Ghica family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghica_family "Ghica family"), [George Ghica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Ghica "George Ghica"). In the early 1680s, Moldavian troops under [George Ducas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Ducas "George Ducas") intervened in [right-bank Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right-bank_Ukraine "Right-bank Ukraine") and assisted [Mehmed IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmed_IV "Mehmed IV") in the [Battle of Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vienna "Battle of Vienna"), only to suffer the effects of the [Great Turkish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Turkish_War "Great Turkish War").

### Phanariots (1711–1822)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Phanariots (1711–1822)")]

Main articles: [Phanariotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phanariotes "Phanariotes") and [Russo-Turkish wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_wars "Russo-Turkish wars")

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Principati1786.jpg/250px-Principati1786.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Principati1786.jpg)

The Principalities of Moldavia and [Wallachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallachia "Wallachia") in 1782, Italian map by G. Pittori, since the geographer Giovanni Antonio Rizzi Zannoni

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Siege_and_capture_of_Jassy_in_1788_by_the_Russian_army.jpg/250px-Siege_and_capture_of_Jassy_in_1788_by_the_Russian_army.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Siege_and_capture_of_Jassy_in_1788_by_the_Russian_army.jpg)

The siege and capture of [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași") by the Russian Army during the [Russo-Turkish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1787%E2%80%931792) "Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792)") in 1788

During the late 17th century, Moldavia became the target of the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire")'s southwards expansion, inaugurated by [Peter the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great "Peter the Great") with the [Russo-Turkish War of 1710-1711](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pruth_River_Campaign "Pruth River Campaign"). Prince [Dimitrie Cantemir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitrie_Cantemir "Dimitrie Cantemir") sided with Peter in open rebellion against the Ottomans, but he was defeated at [Stănilești](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St%C4%83nile%C8%99ti "Stănilești"). Sultan [Ahmed III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_III "Ahmed III") officially discarded recognition of local choices for princes, imposing instead a system relying solely on Ottoman approval: the [Phanariote epoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phanariotes "Phanariotes"), inaugurated by the reign of [Nicholas Mavrocordatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Mavrocordatos "Nicholas Mavrocordatos").

Phanariote rule was marked by [political corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption "Political corruption"), intrigue, and high taxation, as well as by sporadic incursions of Habsburg and Russian armies deep into Moldavian territory. Nonetheless, they also attempted legislative and administrative modernization inspired by [The Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") (such as the decision by [Constantine Mavrocordatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_Mavrocordatos "Constantine Mavrocordatos") to salarize public offices, to the outrage of boyars, and the abolition of serfdom in 1749, as well as [Scarlat Callimachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlat_Callimachi_(hospodar) "Scarlat Callimachi (hospodar)")'s _Code_), and signified a decrease in Ottoman demands after the threat of Russian annexation became real and the prospects of a better life led to waves of peasant emigration to neighboring lands. The effects of Ottoman control were also made less notable after the 1774 [Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_K%C3%BC%C3%A7%C3%BCk_Kaynarca "Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca") allowed Russia to intervene in favour of Ottoman subjects of the Eastern Orthodox faith - leading to campaigns of petitioning by the Moldavian boyars against princely policies.

In 1712, [Hotin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khotyn "Khotyn") was taken over by the Ottomans and became part of a defensive system that Moldavian princes were required to maintain, as well as an area for Islamic [colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonization "Colonization") (the [Laz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laz_people "Laz people") community).

### Fragmentation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Fragmentation")]

See also: [Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_K%C3%BC%C3%A7%C3%BCk_Kaynarca "Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca") and [Treaty of Bucharest (1812)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Bucharest_(1812) "Treaty of Bucharest (1812)")

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Rom1793-1812.png/250px-Rom1793-1812.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rom1793-1812.png)

The Principality of Moldavia, 1793–1812, highlighted in orange

In 1775, Moldavia ceded to the [Habsburg Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_monarchy "Habsburg monarchy") its northwestern part, which became known as [Bukovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukovina "Bukovina"). The Ottomans protested, but consequently, in order to avoid another war, agreed to relinquish the territory. Under the Austro-Ottoman Convention of [Pera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beyo%C4%9Flu "Beyoğlu") (modern-day Beyoğlu) on 7 May 1775, the region that came to be known as Bukovina was officially ceded to the Habsburgs. On 2 July 1776, at Palamutka, Austrians and Ottomans signed a border convention, Austria giving back 59 of the previously occupied villages, retaining 278 villages. For Moldavia, it meant both an important territorial loss and a major blow to the cattle trade, as the region stood on the trade route to Central Europe.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-40)

The [Treaty of Jassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Jassy "Treaty of Jassy") in 1792 forced the Ottoman Empire to cede [Yedisan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yedisan "Yedisan") to the Russian Empire. This made Russian presence much more notable, given that the Empire acquired a common border with Moldavia. The first effect of this was the cession of the eastern half of Moldavia (renamed as [Bessarabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessarabia "Bessarabia")) to the Russian Empire in 1812.

### Organic Statute, 1848 revolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Organic Statute, 1848 revolution")]

Main articles: [Regulamentul Organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulamentul_Organic "Regulamentul Organic"), [Moldavian Revolution of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_Revolution_of_1848 "Moldavian Revolution of 1848"), and [Wallachian Revolution of 1848](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallachian_Revolution_of_1848 "Wallachian Revolution of 1848")

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Princely_Court_of_Jassy.jpg/250px-Princely_Court_of_Jassy.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Princely_Court_of_Jassy.jpg)

Iași, [Princely Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Culture_(Ia%C8%99i) "Palace of Culture (Iași)") of Moldavia

Phanariote rule was officially ended after the 1821 occupation of the country by [Alexander Ypsilantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ypsilantis "Alexander Ypsilantis")'s [Filiki Eteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filiki_Eteria "Filiki Eteria") during the [Greek War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_War_of_Independence "Greek War of Independence"); the subsequent Ottoman retaliation led to the rule of [Ioan Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioan_Sturdza "Ioan Sturdza"). He was considered the first of a new system, since the Ottomans and Russia had agreed in 1826 to allow for the election by locals of rulers over the two [Danubian Principalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danubian_Principalities "Danubian Principalities"), and convened on their mandating for seven-year terms. In practice, a new foundation to reigns in Moldavia was created by the [Russo-Turkish War (1828–1829)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1828%E2%80%931829) "Russo-Turkish War (1828–1829)"), beginning a period of Russian domination over the two countries which ended only in 1856. Begun as a military occupation under the command of [Pavel Kiselyov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavel_Kiselyov "Pavel Kiselyov"), Russian domination gave Wallachia and Moldavia, which were not removed from nominal Ottoman control, the modernizing _[Organic Statute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulamentul\_Organic "Regulamentul Organic")_ (the first document resembling a [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution "Constitution"), as well as the first to regard both principalities). After 1829, the country also became an important destination for [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration") of [Ashkenazi Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jews "Ashkenazi Jews") from the [Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Galicia_and_Lodomeria "Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria") and areas of Russia (_see [History of the Jews in Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History\_of\_the\_Jews\_in\_Romania "History of the Jews in Romania") and [Sudiți](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudi%C8%9Bi "Sudiți")_).

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Obeliscul_cu_lei_Iasi_02.JPG/250px-Obeliscul_cu_lei_Iasi_02.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Obeliscul_cu_lei_Iasi_02.JPG)

Iași, [Obelisk of Lions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copou_Park "Copou Park") (1834), dedicated to the Organic Statute

The first Moldavian rule established under the Statute, that of [Mihail Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Sturdza "Mihail Sturdza"), was nonetheless ambivalent: eager to reduce abuse of office, Sturdza introduced reforms (the abolition of slavery, [secularization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularization "Secularization"), economic rebuilding), but he was widely seen as enforcing his own power over that of the newly instituted consultative Assembly. A supporter of the union of his country with Wallachia and of Romanian [Romantic nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_nationalism "Romantic nationalism"), he obtained the establishment of a [customs union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customs_union "Customs union") between the two countries (1847) and showed support for [radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radicalism_(historical) "Radicalism (historical)") projects favored by low boyars; nevertheless, he clamped down with noted violence the [Moldavian revolutionary attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallachian_Revolution_of_1848 "Wallachian Revolution of 1848") in the last days of March 1848. [Grigore Alexandru Ghica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grigore_Alexandru_Ghica "Grigore Alexandru Ghica") allowed the exiled revolutionaries to return to Moldavia c. 1853, which led to the creation of the [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_(Romania) "National Party (Romania)") (_Partida Națională_), a trans-boundary group of radical union supporters which campaigned for a single state under a foreign dynasty.

### Union with Wallachia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Union with Wallachia")]

Main article: [Unification of Moldavia and Wallachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Moldavia_and_Wallachia "Unification of Moldavia and Wallachia")

Russian domination ended abruptly after the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War"), when the Treaty of Paris also passed the two Romanian principalities under the tutelage of [Great European Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_power "Great power") (together with Russia and the Ottoman overlord, power-sharing included the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, the [Austrian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Empire "Austrian Empire"), the [French Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_Empire "Second French Empire"), the [Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Piedmont-Sardinia "Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia"), and [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia "Prussia")). Due to Austrian and Ottoman opposition and British reserves, the union program as demanded by radical campaigners was debated intensely.

In September 1857, given that _[Caimacam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaymakam "Kaymakam")_[Nicolae Vogoride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Vogoride "Nicolae Vogoride") had perpetrated [fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud") in elections in Moldavia, the Powers allowed the two states to convene ad hoc [divans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divan "Divan"), which were to decide a new constitutional framework; the result showed overwhelming support for the union, as the creation of a [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism") and [neutral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutrality_(international_relations) "Neutrality (international relations)") state. After further meetings among leaders of tutor states, an agreement was reached (the _Paris Convention_), whereby a limited union was to be enforced – separate governments and thrones, with only two bodies in common (a [Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Cassation_and_Justice "High Court of Cassation and Justice") and a Central Commission residing in [Focșani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foc%C8%99ani "Focșani")); it also stipulated that an end to all privilege was to be passed into law, and awarded back to Moldavia the areas around [Bolhrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolhrad "Bolhrad"), [Cahul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cahul "Cahul"), and [Izmail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izmail "Izmail").

However, the Convention failed to note whether the two thrones could not be occupied by the same person, allowing _Partida Națională_ to introduce the candidacy of [Alexandru Ioan Cuza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza "Alexandru Ioan Cuza") in both countries. On January 17 (January 5, 1859, [Old Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption_of_the_Gregorian_calendar#Adoption_in_Eastern_Europe "Adoption of the Gregorian calendar")), in [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași"), he was elected prince of Moldavia by the respective electoral body. After street pressure over the much more [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism") body in [Bucharest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest "Bucharest"), Cuza was elected in Wallachia as well (February 5/January 24), this being considered as the day of the [unification of Moldavia and Wallachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_of_Moldavia_and_Wallachia "Unification of Moldavia and Wallachia") by means of a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union").

In 1862, after diplomatic missions that helped remove opposition to the action, the [United Principalities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Principalities "United Principalities") (the basis of modern Romania) was formally created, and instituted Cuza as _[Domnitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domnitor "Domnitor")_ – thus officially ending the existence of the Principality of Moldavia. All other pending legal matters were clarified after the replacement of Cuza with [Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_I_of_Romania "Carol I of Romania") in April 1866, and the creation of an independent [Kingdom of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Romania "Kingdom of Romania") in 1881.

Nomadic [Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma_minority_in_Romania "Roma minority in Romania") family traveling in Moldavia, [Auguste Raffet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Raffet "Auguste Raffet"), 1837

Slavery ([Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language"): _robie_) was part of the [social order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_class "Social class") from before the founding of the Principality of Moldavia, until it was [abolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism "Abolitionism") in stages during the 1840s and 1850s. Most of the slaves were of [Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma_minority_in_Romania "Roma minority in Romania") (Gypsy) ethnicity. There were also slaves of [Tatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars") ethnicity, probably prisoners captured from the wars. The institution of slavery was first attested in a 1470 Moldavian document, through which Prince [Stephen the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_III_of_Moldavia "Stephen III of Moldavia") frees Oană, a Tatar slave who had fled to [Jagiellon Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Poland_during_the_Jagiellon_dynasty "History of Poland during the Jagiellon dynasty").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Achim-42)

The exact origins of slavery are not known, as it was a common [practice in medieval Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_medieval_Europe "Slavery in medieval Europe"). As in the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"), the Roma were held as slaves of the state, of the [boyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyars "Boyars") or of the monasteries. Historian [Nicolae Iorga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolae_Iorga "Nicolae Iorga") associated the Roma people's arrival with the 1241 [Mongol invasion of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Europe "Mongol invasion of Europe") and considered their slavery as a vestige of that era; he believed that the Romanians took the Roma as slaves from the [Mongols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongols "Mongols") and preserved their status to control their labor. Other historians consider that the Roma were enslaved while captured during the battles with the Tatars. The practice of enslaving prisoners may also have been taken from the Mongols. The ethnic identity of the "Tatar slaves" is unknown, they could have been captured Tatars of the [Golden Horde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horde "Golden Horde"), [Cumans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuman_people "Cuman people"), or the slaves of Tatars and Cumans.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Achim-42) While it is possible that some Romani people were slaves or auxiliary troops of the Mongols or Tatars, most of them came from south of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube"), demonstrating that slavery was a widespread practice. The Tatar slaves, smaller in numbers, were eventually merged into the Roma population.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Stefanescu-43)

Traditionally, Roma slaves were divided into three categories. The smallest was owned by the _hospodars_, and went by the Romanian-language name of _țigani domnești_ ("Gypsies belonging to the lord"). The two other categories comprised _țigani mănăstirești_ ("Gypsies belonging to the monasteries"), who were the property of [Romanian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Orthodox_Church "Romanian Orthodox Church") and [Greek Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Orthodox_Church "Greek Orthodox Church") monasteries, and _țigani boierești_ ("Gypsies belonging to the boyars"), who were enslaved by the category of landowners.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Djuvara-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Guy-45)

The abolition of slavery was carried out following a campaign by young revolutionaries who embraced the [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism "Liberalism") ideas of the [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment"). In 1844, Moldavian Prince [Mihail Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Sturdza "Mihail Sturdza") proposed a law on the freeing of slaves owned by the church and state. By the 1850s, the movement gained support from almost the whole of Romanian society. In December 1855, following a proposal by Prince [Grigore Alexandru Ghica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grigore_Alexandru_Ghica "Grigore Alexandru Ghica"), a bill drafted by [Mihail Kogălniceanu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Kog%C4%83lniceanu "Mihail Kogălniceanu") and [Petre Mavrogheni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petre_Mavrogheni "Petre Mavrogheni") was adopted by the Divan; the law emancipated all slaves to the status of taxpayers (citizens).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Achim-42)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Djuvara-44)

Support for the abolitionists was reflected in [Romanian literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_literature "Romanian literature") of the mid-19th century. The issue of the Roma slavery became a theme in the literary works of various [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_and_radicalism_in_Romania "Liberalism and radicalism in Romania") and [Romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism") intellectuals, many of whom were active in the abolitionist camp. The Romanian abolitionist movement was also influenced by the much larger movement against [Black slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States") in the United States through press reports and through a translation of [Harriet Beecher Stowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Beecher_Stowe "Harriet Beecher Stowe")'s _[Uncle Tom's Cabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Tom's\_Cabin "Uncle Tom's Cabin")_. Translated by Theodor Codrescu and first published in [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași") in 1853, under the name _Coliba lui Moșu Toma sau Viața negrilor în sudul Statelor Unite din America_ (which translates back as "Uncle Toma's Cabin or the Life of Blacks in the Southern United States of America"), it was the first American novel to be published in Romanian. The foreword included a study on slavery by Mihail Kogălniceanu.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-Achim-42)

## Military forces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Military forces")]

Main article: [Moldavian military forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_military_forces "Moldavian military forces")

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Kingdom_of_Hungary_against_Moldavians_flag_in_battle.jpg/250px-Kingdom_of_Hungary_against_Moldavians_flag_in_battle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kingdom_of_Hungary_against_Moldavians_flag_in_battle.jpg)

Moldavian troops in battle, as illustrated in [Johannes de Thurocz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_de_Thurocz "Johannes de Thurocz") (1488 edition); the [Moldavian flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_and_coat_of_arms_of_Moldavia "Flag and coat of arms of Moldavia") is displayed.

Under the reign of [Stephen the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_III_of_Moldavia "Stephen III of Moldavia"), all farmers and villagers had to bear arms. Stephen justified this by saying that "every man has a duty to defend his fatherland"; according to Polish chronicler [Jan Długosz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_D%C5%82ugosz "Jan Długosz"), if someone was found without carrying a weapon, he was [sentenced to death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_sentence "Death sentence").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-46) Stephen reformed the army by promoting men from the landed free peasantry _răzeși_ (i.e. something akin to [freeholding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freehold_(law) "Freehold (law)")[yeomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeomen "Yeomen")) to infantry (_voinici_) and light cavalry (_hânsari_), reducing his dependence on the [boyars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyars "Boyars"), and introduced guns. The Small Host (_Oastea Mică_) consisted of around 10,000 to 12,000 men. The Large Host (_Oastea Mare_), which could reach up to 40,000, was recruited from all the free peasantry older than 14 and strong enough to carry a [sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword "Sword") or use a [bow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_(weapon) "Bow (weapon)"). This seldom happened, for such a [levée en masse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev%C3%A9e_en_masse "Levée en masse") was devastating for both economy and population growth. In the [Battle of Vaslui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vaslui "Battle of Vaslui"), Stephen had to summon the Large Host and also recruited [mercenary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary "Mercenary") troops.

In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages") and early [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance"), the Moldavians relied on light [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") (_[călărași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C4%83l%C4%83ra%C8%99i\_(cavalry)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Călărași (cavalry) (page does not exist)")_) which used [hit-and-run tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit-and-run_tactics "Hit-and-run tactics") similar to those of the [Tatars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatars "Tatars"); this gave them great mobility and also flexibility, in case they found it more suitable to dismount their horses and fight in hand-to-hand combat, as it happened in 1422, when 400 [horse archers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_archer "Horse archer") were sent to aid [Jagiellon Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Poland_(1385%E2%80%931569) "History of Poland (1385–1569)"), Moldavia's overlord against the [Teutonic Knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teutonic_Knights "Teutonic Knights"). When making eye-contact with the enemy, the horse archers would withdraw to a nearby forest and [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camouflage "Camouflage") themselves with leaves and branches; according to Jan Długosz, when the enemy entered the wood, they were "showered with arrows" and defeated.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-47) The heavy cavalry consisted of the nobility, namely, the boyars, and their guards, the _viteji_ (lit. "brave ones", small nobility) and the _curteni_ (court cavalry). These were all nominally part of the Small Host. In times of war, boyars were compelled by the [feudal system of allegiance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism") to supply the prince with troops in accordance with the extent of their [manorial domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manorialism "Manorialism").

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Modovian_army_-_Kronika_tho_iesth_Historya_swiata_1564_%28109729892%29.jpg/250px-Modovian_army_-_Kronika_tho_iesth_Historya_swiata_1564_%28109729892%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modovian_army_-_Kronika_tho_iesth_Historya_swiata_1564_(109729892).jpg)

Moldavian troops engaging the Poles in the [Battle of Obertyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Obertyn "Battle of Obertyn"), 1531

Other troops consisted of professional foot soldiers (_lefegii_) which fulfilled the [heavy infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_infantry#Middle_Ages "Heavy infantry") role, and the _plăieși_, free peasants whose role was that of border guards: they guarded the mountain passes and were prepared to [ambush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush "Ambush") the enemy and to fight delaying actions.

In the absence of the prince, command was assigned to the _Mare Spătar_ (Grand Sword-Bearer, a military office) or to the _Mare Vornic_ (approx. Governor of the Country; a civilian office second only to the _[Voievod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voievod#Moldavia\_and\_Wallachia "Voievod")_, which was filled by the prince himself). Supplying the troops was by tradition-later-made-into-law the duty of the inhabitants of those lands on which the soldiers were present at a given time.

The Moldavians' (as well as Wallachians') favourite military doctrine in (defensive) wars was a [scorched earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorched_earth "Scorched earth") policy combined with harassment of the advancing enemy using [hit-and-run tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit-and-run_tactics "Hit-and-run tactics") and disruption of communication and supply lines, followed by a large scale ambush: a weakened enemy would be lured in a place where it would find itself in a position hard or impossible to defend. A general attack would follow, often with devastating results. The shattered remains of what was once the enemy army would be pursued closely and harassed all the way to the border and sometimes beyond. A typical example of successful employments of this scenario is the [Battle of Vaslui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Vaslui "Battle of Vaslui").

Towards the end of the 15th century, especially after the success of [guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun "Gun") and [cannons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannon "Cannon"), mercenaries became a dominant force in the country's military. With the economic demands created by the [stagnation of the Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagnation_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "Stagnation of the Ottoman Empire"), the force diminished and included only mercenaries such as the _[seimeni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seimeni "Seimeni")_.

The 1829 [Treaty of Adrianople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Adrianople_(1829) "Treaty of Adrianople (1829)") allowed Moldavia to again maintain its own troops, no longer acting as an auxiliary under strict Ottoman supervision, and assigned red over blue [pennants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_terminology "Flag terminology") (_see [Flag and coat of arms of Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag\_and\_coat\_of\_arms\_of\_Moldavia "Flag and coat of arms of Moldavia")_). Their renewed existence under [Mihail Sturdza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihail_Sturdza "Mihail Sturdza") was a major symbol and rally point for the [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_nationalism "Romantic nationalism") cause, aiding in bringing about the [1848 Moldavian revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1848_Moldavian_revolution "1848 Moldavian revolution").

### Fleet

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Fleet")]

An early mention of a Moldavian [naval fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_fleet "Naval fleet") is found in connection with the rule of [Aron Tiranul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aron_Tiranul "Aron Tiranul"), who used it to help [Wallachian ruler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_rulers_of_Wallachia "List of rulers of Wallachia")[Michael the Brave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_the_Brave "Michael the Brave") establish his control over the [Chilia branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilia_branch "Chilia branch") of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") and [Dobruja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobruja "Dobruja").

The Treaty of Adrianople provided for a Moldavian self-defense naval force, to be composed of [caicque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caicque "Caicque") vessels. [Schooners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schooner "Schooner") armed with [cannons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannon "Cannon") were first built in the 1840s. Along with patrolling the Danube, these made their way on its tributaries, the [Siret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siret_River "Siret River") and the [Prut River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prut_River "Prut River").

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Geography")]

See also: [Moldavian Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavian_Plateau "Moldavian Plateau")

Geographically, Moldavia is limited by the [Carpathian Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains "Carpathian Mountains") to the West, the [Cheremosh River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheremosh_River "Cheremosh River") to the North, the [Dniester River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dniester_River "Dniester River") to the East and the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") and [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea") to the South. The [Prut River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prut_River "Prut River") flows approximately through its middle from north to south.

Of late 15th century Moldavia, with an area of 94,862 km 2 (36,626 sq mi),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-histmold-48) the biggest part and the core of the former principality is located in Romania (45.6%), followed by the [Republic of Moldova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Moldova "Republic of Moldova") (31.7%), and Ukraine (22.7%). This represents 88.2% of the Republic of Moldova's surface, 18% of Romania's surface, and 3.5% of Ukraine's surface.

The region is mostly hilly, with a range of mountains in the west, and plain areas in the southeast. Moldavia's highest altitude is [Ineu peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineu_Peak "Ineu Peak") (2,279 m), which is also the westernmost point of the region.

The parts of Moldavia populated by [Csángó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cs%C3%A1ng%C3%B3s "Csángós")[Hungarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarians "Hungarians") are sometimes referred to as [Csángó Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cs%C3%A1ng%C3%B3_Land "Csángó Land").

See also: [Demographic history of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_history_of_Romania "Demographic history of Romania"), [Bessarabia §Population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessarabia#Population "Bessarabia"), [Bukovina §Historical population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukovina#Historical_population "Bukovina"), [Chernivtsi Oblast §Population and demographics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernivtsi_Oblast#Population_and_demographics "Chernivtsi Oblast"), and [Budjak §Ethnic groups and demographics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budjak#Ethnic_groups_and_demographics "Budjak")

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Moldo-Wallachian_Peasantry%2C_1853.jpg/250px-Moldo-Wallachian_Peasantry%2C_1853.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moldo-Wallachian_Peasantry,_1853.jpg)

Moldo-Wallachian peasantry, 1853

Contemporary historians estimate the population (historically referred to as Moldavians) of the Moldavian Principality in the 15th century, at between 250,000 and 600,000 people,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-49)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-50) but an extensive census was first conducted in 1769–1774.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-51)

In 1848, the northwestern part, annexed in 1775 by the Habsburg Empire, [Bukovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukovina "Bukovina"), had a population of 377,571; in 1856, the eastern half of Moldavia, [Bessarabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessarabia "Bessarabia"), annexed in 1812 by the Russian Empire, had a population of 990,274, while the population of Moldavia proper (the western half), in 1859, was 1,463,927.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-52)

The contemporary population peaked in 1992, at 10.07 million inhabitants in all three historical divisions ([Western Moldavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Moldavia "Western Moldavia"), Bessarabia and Bukovina). As of 2011, the population was 8.63 million people, of which 3.67 million were in Western Moldavia, 3.86 million in Bessarabia and 1.08 million in Bukovina.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-histmold-48)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Moldavia&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Education")]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/AcademiaMihaileana.jpg/250px-AcademiaMihaileana.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AcademiaMihaileana.jpg)

[Academia Mihăileană](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academia_Mih%C4%83ilean%C4%83 "Academia Mihăileană") was the first modern institution of higher learning in Moldavia.

In 1562, the so-called [Schola Latina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioan_Iacob_Heraclid "Ioan Iacob Heraclid") (a Latin Academic College) was founded in [Cotnari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotnari "Cotnari"), near [Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ia%C8%99i "Iași"), a school which marked the beginnings of the organized humanistic education institutions in Moldavia.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-53)

The first institute of higher learning that functioned on the territory of Romania was [Academia Vasiliană](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasilian_College "Vasilian College") (1640),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-54) founded by Prince Vasile Lupu as a _Higher School for Latin and Slavonic Languages_, followed by the [Princely Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_Academy,_Ia%C8%99i "Princely Academy, Iași"), in 1707. The first high education structure in [Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language "Romanian language") was established in the autumn of 1813, when [Gheorghe Asachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gheorghe_Asachi "Gheorghe Asachi") laid the foundations of a class of engineers, its activities taking place within the Greek Princely Academy.

After 1813, other moments marked the development of higher education in Romanian, regarding both [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") and the technical science. [Academia Mihăileană](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academia_Mih%C4%83ilean%C4%83 "Academia Mihăileană"), founded in 1835 by Prince Mihail Sturdza, is considered the first Romanian superior institute. In 1860, three faculties part of the Academia Mihăileană formed the nucleus for the newly established [University of Iași](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandru_Ioan_Cuza_University "Alexandru Ioan Cuza University"), the first Romanian modern university.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldavia#cite_note-55)

The **Vasile Alecsandri National Theatre** ([Romanian](link_13): _Teatrul Național „Vasile Alecsandri” din Bălți_) in [Bălți](link_0), is one of the national theatres of [Moldova](link_9). Founded in 1957, it was given the name of the renowned Romanian playwright and poet [Vasile Alecsandri](link_3). On 26 January 1990,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%83l%C8%9Bi_National_Theatre#cite_note-history-1) Vasile Alecsandri Theatre became the first national theatre in Moldova.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C4%83l%C8%9Bi_National_Theatre#cite_note-2)
